This shouldn't be much of a surprise.

The x86 architecture has survived as long as it did for a few reasons. One of the most important of these was backwards compatibility. There have been many other architectures that wanted to "take over" for the x86. Intel launched two itself, one of which being the infamous Itanium, which is better known in some circles as the "Itanic," which should indicate just how well it went for the most part. Just about all of them failed, even the ones that claimed to have perfect compatibility via software and emulation. Intel's refrain of the Itanium having emulation that offered "almost" the same performance and capability as true x86 chip was insufficient; if it were there's a decent chance that we'd all be running Itanium-based 64-bit hardware instead of a 64-bit instruction set that was extended from the existing x86 32-bit base by AMD.

And now Microsoft is desperate to lock everyone into Windows 10, whether anyone wants it or not, along with all the nasty implications it brings to the table. But tablets and phones are coming up, and PCs and laptops aren't looking so hot. They're hardly going away any time soon, but they're also going to have a lot more competition for a portion of a customer's budget that probably hasn't grown all that much. So Intel is faced with a choice - kowtow to Microsoft and bind their fate to Windows as well, or retain the primary underlying benefit of their architecture.

It shouldn't be a surprise that they are not too hot for locking in software.

In fact, if Microsoft was seriously counting on that, they were completely mad - Windows has been ported to different architectures, so they've shown they really don't have any sort of unswerving loyalty to x86 or Intel.
